problem: The AI states what it can and cannot do outside the host's own data without a source of truth for it: it describes a capability that does not exist, reports a setting as blocking when the setting was never read, or says outside work has started when nothing ran. It also says it cannot do something it can.
who_has_it: People who rely on the AI to say what it can do for them, and operators who connect external environments to it.
why_it_matters: In production one person was told about a submission script that does not exist, two others were told AI work was switched off in their settings when the request could have been done, and a reply announced a background task that was never queued. A false capability or a false blocker ends trust faster than a plain no.
why_hard: What is reachable changes per person, team and deployment (connected environments, allowlisted tools and servers, what a setting allows), the inventory lives in the host, and a model fills a gap in its prompt with a plausible capability.
existing_attempts: The host's reach summary and a stronger-tier reach judge before planning (core/reach_judge.py, off by default); the tool catalog's when-to-use text; the answer check that flags claims of unexecuted work.

problem: Deep work can start from a task description with no written, checkable condition for finishing, so the run plans forward from its first step and has nothing to be checked against when it stops.
who_has_it: People who hand the AI open-ended work, and the verifier that has to judge the result afterwards.
why_it_matters: Without a done-standard the verifier can only restate the task, so a run can end on effort instead of on the goal being met, and the person finds the gap later.
why_hard: A person's request is often short or loose, a good done-standard must be checkable without being narrower than the ask, and deriving one costs a model call that a self-contained request does not need.
existing_attempts: A model call that derives a short checkable done-standard from a request, a worker prompt that puts the done-standard beside the task, and the goal loop that verifies the result against it and re-runs while it is unmet.

problem: A new goal is given to the wrong owner, or to an AI representative that cannot do it, so it sits undone or is done badly while the person believes it is handled.
who_has_it: People who create goals for themselves, their team or an AI representative.
why_it_matters: A goal nobody can actually do looks owned, so it stalls without anyone noticing, and a goal taken over by an AI that cannot do it comes back as wasted spend.
why_hard: Who a goal belongs to is written in free text, whether an AI can do it depends on what it can reach, and asking the person every time is its own failure.
existing_attempts: A person assigning by hand, and a fast-model check of who a goal fits and whether an AI representative can take it over.

problem: What the AI says about the person's own account (which quests exist, what changed, whether a change ran) is re-derived each turn from whatever slice it read, and a change it made is not read back, so within one session it reports the same state two ways, repeats a change it already made, or proposes again what it said was done.
who_has_it: People who ask the AI to change their quests and then ask what state they are in.
why_it_matters: In production one account's quests were described as a single completed goal and then as four initialised quests within ten minutes, and the person asked what state the account was in four separate times. An assistant that cannot report its own state cannot be trusted to change it.
why_hard: The host's data changes from many places (the app, other people, background work), a card or cache of it lags, a read on every turn costs time, and a library that serves any host cannot assume one data model.
existing_attempts: A managed card per quest rebuilt on sync, through which a turn is grounded in its quest; live reads through the host's retrieval adapter; the quest change executor and its final-state metric; the answer check that flags claims of unexecuted work.

problem: Quest's operations can be reached in the same process as Quest and over its HTTP API, and two access points to the same operations can drift apart, so the same request may behave or return differently depending on how it arrived.
who_has_it: Developers of Quest and of the runner, and people whose requests reach Quest AI through either path.
why_it_matters: If the two paths differ, a change that works in one fails or behaves differently in the other, and fixes made at one access point never reach the other.
why_hard: The two paths are separate code (the HTTP client in the runner and the embedded access inside Quest) with different failure modes (a network can fail after a write is sent), so sameness has to be kept by contract and checked, not assumed.
existing_attempts: One client contract in which every write returns a typed result or raises and never returns an empty value; the written API contract that the client follows; the HTTP client built from the environment. No comparison of the two paths exists yet.
